passage_text: Researchers investigated the impact of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance in adolescents aged 13–17. The study recruited 120 participants and randomly assigned them to one of four sleep conditions: 8 hours, 6 hours, 4 hours, and 2 hours of sleep per night for a week. Each group completed a standardized reaction time task and a memory accuracy test at the end of the week. The researchers recorded mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and accuracy percentages for each group. The data suggested a clear trend: as sleep duration decreased, reaction times increased and accuracy declined. The authors concluded that adequate sleep is essential for optimal cognitive functioning in this age group and recommended policy changes to promote longer sleep durations among adolescents.
stem: Which sleep condition produced the fastest mean reaction time?
explanation: The table shows the lowest reaction time (350 ms) for the 8‑hour sleep group, indicating the fastest response.
trap: Students often confuse fastest reaction time with highest accuracy.

stem: Which experimental design best supports a causal claim that sleep duration affects cognitive performance?
explanation: Random assignment to sleep conditions controls for confounding variables, allowing causal inference.
trap: Students may think a longitudinal study provides causality, but it only shows association.

stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable if it differed systematically across the four sleep groups?

options.A: Caffeine intake, if shorter sleepers drank more caffeine to stay awake
options.B: The use of the same standardized reaction-time task in every group
options.C: Equal sample size (30) in each group
options.D: Random assignment of participants to the sleep conditions

explanation: Correct: A confounder varies with the exposure and independently affects the outcome; caffeine could speed reaction time and differ with sleep hours. Why the others are wrong: B) A task identical across groups is a constant and cannot create a group difference. C) Equal group sizes are not a variable related to reaction time. D) Random assignment is a design feature that reduces confounding, not a confounder.
trap: Selecting a design feature that is held constant as if it were a source of bias.

stem: Which statement best links the study’s findings to real‑world implications for adolescent health policy?

options.A: Sleep deprivation has no measurable effect on adolescent cognitive performance.
options.B: Shorter sleep led to slower reactions and lower accuracy, which supports promoting longer sleep in adolescents.
options.C: Only reaction time, not accuracy, is affected by sleep duration.
options.D: Sleep duration is irrelevant to educational outcomes.

explanation: Correct: Reaction time rose (350 to 520 ms) and accuracy fell (95 to 80%) as sleep decreased from 8 to 2 hours, supporting the recommendation for longer sleep. Why the others are wrong: A) the data show clear effects of sleep loss. C) accuracy also declined with less sleep, so reaction time was not the only measure affected. D) the study did not measure educational outcomes, so no conclusion about their irrelevance follows.
trap: Dismissing the accuracy decline as unimportant, or claiming the study shows nothing for health policy.
